chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — A Desert Place
paragraphs: [Thunder and Lightning. Enter three Witches.]
FIRST WITCH. When will the three of us meet again? In thunder, lightning, or in rain?
SECOND WITCH. When the chaos of battle is over. When one side has lost and the other has won.
THIRD WITCH. That will be before the sun goes down.
FIRST WITCH. Where shall we meet?
SECOND WITCH. On the heath.
THIRD WITCH. There we'll meet Macbeth.
FIRST WITCH. I'm coming, Graymalkin!
SECOND WITCH. My toad is calling.
THIRD WITCH. Coming!
ALL. What's fair is foul, and what's foul is fair. Let us fly through the fog and the filthy air.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — A Camp near Forres
paragraphs: [Alarum within. Enter King Duncan, Malcolm, Donalbain, Lennox, with Attendants, meeting a bleeding Captain.]
DUNCAN. Who is that bloody man? From the look of him, he can give us the latest news of the rebellion.
MALCOLM. This is the sergeant who fought bravely to keep me from being captured. Hail, brave friend! Tell the King what was happening in the battle when you left it.

SOLDIER. It was hanging in the balance, like two exhausted swimmers clinging to each other and dragging each other down. The ruthless Macdonwald, who deserves to be called a rebel since every kind of villainy swarms around him, had been supplied with foot soldiers and heavily armed fighters from the Western Isles. And Fortune seemed to smile on his damned cause, like a rebel's whore. But none of that was enough. Brave Macbeth, who well deserves that name, scorning Fortune, carved his way through with his blood-smoking sword, like Valor's favorite warrior, until he stood face to face with Macdonwald. He didn't shake his hand or say goodbye. He split him open from the navel to the jaw and stuck his head on our battlements.
DUNCAN. Oh, valiant cousin! What a worthy gentleman!

SOLDIER. But just as storms and terrible thunder break out from the same direction the sun rises, new trouble came from where we thought we'd found relief. Listen carefully, King of Scotland: no sooner had justice, armed with valor, forced those skirmishing soldiers to run for their lives, than the Norwegian lord, seeing his opportunity, launched a fresh attack with polished weapons and fresh troops.
DUNCAN. Didn't this alarm our captains, Macbeth and Banquo?

SOLDIER. About as much as sparrows alarm eagles, or a hare alarms a lion. To tell the truth, they were like cannons loaded with double charges. They redoubled their blows against the enemy. It seemed as if they meant to bathe in steaming wounds or make the battlefield another Golgotha. I can't say more. I'm faint, and my wounds need attention.
DUNCAN. Your words suit you as well as your wounds. They both speak of honor. Go, get him surgeons.
[Exit Captain, attended.]
[Enter Ross and Angus.]
MALCOLM. The worthy Thane of Ross.
LENNOX. What urgency shows in his eyes! He looks like a man who has strange things to report.
ROSS. God save the King!
DUNCAN. Where have you come from, worthy thane?

ROSS. From Fife, great King, where the Norwegian banners taunt the sky and chill our people with fear. Norway himself, with terrible numbers, aided by that most disloyal traitor the Thane of Cawdor, began a grim battle. But Macbeth, like the god of war's own champion, clad in proven armor, met the Norwegian blow for blow, sword against sword, curbing his wild aggression. And to make a long story short, the victory fell to us.
DUNCAN. What wonderful news!
ROSS. And now Sweno, the King of Norway, begs for a peace treaty. We wouldn't even let him bury his dead until he paid us ten thousand dollars at Saint Colme's Inch for our general use.
DUNCAN. The Thane of Cawdor will never again betray our trust. Go pronounce his death sentence, and greet Macbeth with his former title.
ROSS. I'll see it done.
DUNCAN. What Cawdor has lost, noble Macbeth has won.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — A Heath
paragraphs: [Thunder. Enter the three Witches.]
FIRST WITCH. Where have you been, sister?
SECOND WITCH. Killing pigs.
THIRD WITCH. And you, sister?

FIRST WITCH. A sailor's wife was sitting with chestnuts in her lap, munching and munching and munching. "Give me some," I said. "Get away from me, witch!" the fat-rumped hag cried. Her husband has sailed off to Aleppo as master of the Tiger. But I'll sail after him in a sieve, and like a rat without a tail, I'll work my mischief, I'll work my mischief, I'll work my mischief.
SECOND WITCH. I'll give you a wind to help.
FIRST WITCH. How kind of you.
THIRD WITCH. And I'll give you another.

FIRST WITCH. I already control all the rest, and every port they blow toward, every direction on the sailor's compass. I'll drain him dry as hay. Sleep shall hang on his eyelids neither night nor day. He'll live as a cursed man. For nine times nine weary weeks he'll waste away and wither. Though his ship can't be lost, it will be tossed by storms. Look what I have.
SECOND WITCH. Show me, show me.
FIRST WITCH. Here I have a pilot's thumb, wrecked as he was sailing home.
[Drum within.]
THIRD WITCH. A drum, a drum! Macbeth is coming.

ALL. The Weird Sisters, hand in hand, swift travelers over sea and land, go round and round like this: three times for you, three times for me, and three times more to make up nine. Quiet! The spell is ready.
[Enter Macbeth and Banquo.]
MACBETH. I've never seen a day so foul and fair at the same time.

BANQUO. How far is it supposed to be to Forres? What are these creatures, so withered and wild in their appearance, that they don't look like they belong on this earth, and yet here they are? Are you alive? Can you be spoken to? You seem to understand me, each one laying a bony finger on her skinny lips. You look like you should be women, and yet your beards make it hard to believe you are.
MACBETH. Speak, if you can. What are you?
FIRST WITCH. All hail, Macbeth! Hail to you, Thane of Glamis!
SECOND WITCH. All hail, Macbeth! Hail to you, Thane of Cawdor!
THIRD WITCH. All hail, Macbeth! You shall be king hereafter!

BANQUO. My good sir, why do you flinch and seem afraid of things that sound so promising? In the name of truth, are you supernatural beings, or are you actually what you appear to be? You greet my noble partner with his present title and a grand prophecy of noble rank and royal destiny, so that he seems lost in thought. But you say nothing to me. If you can see into the seeds of time and tell which ones will grow and which will not, then speak to me as well. I neither beg for your favor nor fear your hatred.
FIRST WITCH. Hail!
SECOND WITCH. Hail!
THIRD WITCH. Hail!
FIRST WITCH. Lesser than Macbeth, and greater.
SECOND WITCH. Not so fortunate, yet much more fortunate.
THIRD WITCH. You shall father kings, though you will not be one yourself. So all hail, Macbeth and Banquo!
FIRST WITCH. Banquo and Macbeth, all hail!

MACBETH. Wait, you incomplete prophets, tell me more. Through my father Sinel's death, I know I am Thane of Glamis. But how can I be Thane of Cawdor? The Thane of Cawdor is alive and thriving. And to be king is no more within the realm of possibility than to be Cawdor. Tell me where you got this strange knowledge, or why you stop us on this desolate heath with such a prophetic greeting. Speak, I command you.
[Witches vanish.]
BANQUO. The earth has bubbles, just as water does, and these were some of them. Where have they vanished to?
MACBETH. Into the air. What seemed solid melted away like breath into the wind. I wish they had stayed!
BANQUO. Were such things really here, the things we're talking about? Or have we eaten some poisonous root that drives the mind insane?
MACBETH. Your children shall be kings.
BANQUO. You shall be king.
MACBETH. And Thane of Cawdor too. Wasn't that what they said?
BANQUO. Those were the exact words and tune. Who's coming?
[Enter Ross and Angus.]

ROSS. The King was delighted to receive the news of your success, Macbeth. When he heard about your personal bravery in the fight against the rebels, his amazement and his desire to praise you competed with each other. Struck silent by that, when he looked at the rest of that same day's events and found you among the fierce Norwegian ranks, fearless as you dealt out death, reports came flooding in one after another, each one pouring your praises before him for your great defense of the kingdom.
ANGUS. We've been sent to give you the King's thanks, and only to bring you into his presence, not to reward you ourselves.
ROSS. And as a pledge of an even greater honor, the King asked me to call you Thane of Cawdor. So hail to you by that title, most worthy thane, for it is yours.
BANQUO. What, can the devil speak the truth?
MACBETH. The Thane of Cawdor is alive. Why do you dress me in borrowed clothes?

ANGUS. The man who was the Thane is still alive, but he's under a heavy death sentence and deserves to lose his life. Whether he conspired with Norway, or secretly aided the rebel with hidden support, or worked with both to destroy his own country, I don't know. But capital treason, confessed and proven, has overthrown him.

MACBETH. [_Aside._] Glamis, and Thane of Cawdor! The greatest title is still to come. [_To Ross and Angus._] Thank you for your efforts. [_To Banquo._] Don't you hope your children will be kings, since the same ones who gave me the title of Cawdor promised no less to them?

BANQUO. If you trust that prophecy completely, it might fire you up to reach for the crown as well, beyond the title of Cawdor. But it's strange. Often, to lead us to our ruin, the agents of darkness tell us truths about small things, only to betray us when the consequences are greatest. Cousins, a word with you, if I may.

MACBETH. [_Aside._] Two truths have been told, like happy prologues to the grand drama of the crown. I thank you, gentlemen. [_Aside._] This supernatural encouragement can't be evil; it can't be good either. If it's evil, why has it given me a taste of success, beginning with a truth? I am Thane of Cawdor. If it's good, why do I give in to a thought whose horrible image makes my hair stand on end and my steady heart pound against my ribs, against all natural feeling? Present fears are less terrifying than what I'm imagining. The thought of murder is still only a fantasy, yet it shakes my entire being so thoroughly that all normal function is smothered by speculation, and nothing seems real except what doesn't yet exist.
BANQUO. Look how lost in thought our partner is.
MACBETH. [_Aside._] If fate intends to make me king, then fate may crown me without my having to do anything.
BANQUO. New honors fit him like new clothes that don't quite conform to the body until they've been worn awhile.
MACBETH. [_Aside._] Come what may, time moves forward through even the roughest day.
BANQUO. Worthy Macbeth, we're waiting on you whenever you're ready.

MACBETH. Forgive me. My sluggish brain was churning over things half forgotten. Kind gentlemen, your efforts are recorded where I will review them daily. Let us go to the King. Think about what has happened, and when we've had time to consider it, let us speak our minds freely to each other.
BANQUO. Very gladly.
MACBETH. Until then, enough. Come, friends.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4 — Forres. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Flourish. Enter Duncan, Malcolm, Donalbain, Lennox and Attendants.]
DUNCAN. Has the execution of Cawdor been carried out? Haven't those appointed to do it returned yet?

MALCOLM. My lord, they haven't come back yet. But I spoke with someone who saw him die, and he reported that Cawdor very openly confessed his treasons, begged Your Highness's pardon, and showed deep repentance. Nothing in his life became him as well as the way he left it. He died like a man who had rehearsed his death, throwing away the most precious thing he owned as though it were a worthless trifle.
DUNCAN. There is no way to read a man's true nature in his face. He was a gentleman in whom I placed absolute trust.
[Enter Macbeth, Banquo, Ross and Angus.]

MACBETH. The service and loyalty I owe you is its own reward in the doing of it. Your Highness's role is to receive our duties, and our duties are to your throne and state like those of children and servants, who do only what they should by doing everything they can for your love and honor.

DUNCAN. Welcome! I have begun to invest in you, and I will work to see you flourish. Noble Banquo, you have deserved no less, and must be recognized no less for having done so. Let me embrace you and hold you to my heart.
BANQUO. If I grow there, the harvest is yours.

DUNCAN. My overflowing joys, excessive in their fullness, try to hide themselves in tears of happiness. Sons, kinsmen, thanes, and those of you nearest to me, know this: we will establish our succession upon our eldest son, Malcolm, whom we hereby name the Prince of Cumberland. But this honor shall not belong to him alone. Signs of nobility, like stars, shall shine upon all who deserve them. From here, let us travel to Inverness, and deepen our bond with you.
MACBETH. Any rest spent doing something other than serving you is wasted labor. I'll ride ahead myself and bring my wife the joyful news of your approach. So, humbly, I take my leave.
DUNCAN. My worthy Cawdor!

MACBETH. [_Aside._] The Prince of Cumberland! That is a step I must either fall down before or leap over, because it stands in my way. Stars, hide your light! Don't let anyone see my dark and deep desires. Let my eye not see what my hand does, yet let the deed be done that my eye would be afraid to look upon.
[Exit.]
DUNCAN. It's true, worthy Banquo. Macbeth is every bit as valiant as you say, and his praise is a feast to me. Let us follow him. He has raced ahead to prepare our welcome. He is a peerless kinsman.
[Flourish. Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 5 — Inverness. A Room in Macbeth's Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Lady Macbeth, reading a letter.]

LADY MACBETH. "They met me on the day of victory, and I have learned from the most reliable sources that they have powers beyond mortal knowledge. When I burned with desire to question them further, they turned to air and vanished. While I stood there, lost in wonder, messengers arrived from the King who greeted me as 'Thane of Cawdor,' which is exactly what the Weird Sisters had called me before, and they went on to point me toward the future with 'Hail, king that shall be!' I thought it right to share this with you, my dearest partner in greatness, so that you would not miss your rightful share of joy by remaining ignorant of what greatness is promised to you. Keep this close to your heart, and farewell." Glamis you are, and Cawdor, and you shall be what you are promised. Yet I fear your nature. It is too full of the milk of human kindness to take the shortest route. You have ambition, but you lack the ruthlessness that should go with it. What you want greatly, you want to achieve honestly. You would not cheat, and yet you want to win unfairly. You want that which cries, "You must do this if you want me," and yet you are more afraid of doing it than you are of wanting it undone. Hurry home so I can pour my determination into your ear and use the boldness of my tongue to drive away everything that stands between you and the golden crown that fate and supernatural forces seem to have destined for you.
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. The King comes here tonight.
LADY MACBETH. You must be mad to say that! Isn't your master with him? If so, he would have sent word so we could prepare.

MESSENGER. If you please, it is true. Our lord is coming. One of my fellow servants raced ahead of him, and arrived nearly dead from being out of breath, with barely enough left to deliver his message.
LADY MACBETH. Take care of him. He brings great news.
[Exit Messenger.]
[Enter Macbeth.]
MACBETH. My dearest love, Duncan comes here tonight.
LADY MACBETH. And when does he leave?
MACBETH. Tomorrow, as he plans.

LADY MACBETH. Oh, that tomorrow shall never come! Your face, my lord, is like an open book where anyone can read strange things. To deceive the world, look as the world expects you to look. Wear welcome in your eyes, your handshake, your words. Look like the innocent flower, but be the serpent hiding beneath it. The guest who is coming must be provided for, and you shall leave this night's great business in my hands. It will give us absolute power and command over all our nights and days to come.
MACBETH. We will speak more about this.
LADY MACBETH. Just keep a calm, clear expression. To look troubled is to arouse suspicion. Leave all the rest to me.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 6 — Before the Castle
paragraphs: [Hautboys. Servants of Macbeth attending.]
[Enter Duncan, Malcolm, Donalbain, Banquo, Lennox, Macduff, Ross, Angus and Attendants.]
DUNCAN. This castle has a pleasant setting. The air is gentle and sweet to the senses.

BANQUO. This summer visitor, the house martin that loves to nest in temples, proves by choosing to build here that the air of heaven smells inviting. There isn't a ledge, frieze, buttress, or convenient corner where this bird hasn't made its hanging bed and nursery. Where they breed most, I've noticed the air is especially pleasant.
[Enter Lady Macbeth.]

DUNCAN. Look, our honored hostess! The love that follows us sometimes causes us trouble, but we thank it as love all the same. In saying this, I remind you to thank God for the trouble we give you, and to thank us for giving it.

LADY MACBETH. All our service, done twice over in every detail and then doubled again, would be poor and insignificant compared to the deep and broad honors with which Your Majesty loads our house. For the honors of old and the recent dignities heaped upon them, we remain your humble servants.

DUNCAN. Where is the Thane of Cawdor? We followed close behind him and meant to arrive before him as his host, but he rides well. His great love, sharp as his spur, carried him home before us. Fair and noble hostess, we are your guests tonight.
LADY MACBETH. Your servants always hold everything they have, themselves included, in trust, ready to return it all to Your Highness whenever you wish.
DUNCAN. Give me your hand. Lead me to your husband, my host. We value him highly and shall continue to show him our favor. With your permission, hostess.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 7 — A Lobby in the Castle
paragraphs: [Hautboys and torches. Enter, and pass over, a Sewer and divers Servants with dishes and service. Then enter Macbeth.]

MACBETH. If it were truly over and done with once the deed was done, then it would be best to do it quickly. If the assassination could somehow catch all its consequences in a net and guarantee success with Duncan's death; if this one blow could be the beginning and the end of it, right here, right now, on this side of eternity, we'd risk the life to come. But in cases like these, we still face judgment here on earth. We merely teach bloody lessons that, once learned, come back to plague the teacher. This evenhanded justice makes us drink from our own poisoned cup. He is here under double protection: first, I am his kinsman and his subject, both strong reasons against the deed; then, as his host, I should shut the door against his murderer, not carry the knife myself. Besides, this Duncan has worn his power so gently and has been so upright in his great office that his virtues will plead like angels, trumpets blaring, against the damnation of his murder. And pity, like a naked newborn babe riding the storm, or like heaven's angels mounted on the invisible winds, will blow the news of this horrible deed into every eye until tears flood like rain. I have no motivation to drive me forward except leaping ambition, which overreaches itself and falls flat on the other side.
[Enter Lady Macbeth.]
LADY MACBETH. He has nearly finished supper. Why have you left the room?
MACBETH. Has he asked for me?
LADY MACBETH. Don't you know he has?

MACBETH. We will go no further with this plan. He has recently honored me, and I have earned golden opinions from all kinds of people. I want to enjoy them in their fresh newness, not throw them away so soon.

LADY MACBETH. Was the hope you dressed yourself in drunk? Has it been sleeping since? And does it now wake up looking green and pale at what it so freely committed to? From this moment, that is how I will judge your love. Are you afraid to match your actions and courage to your desires? Would you have the thing you consider the greatest prize in life, and yet live as a coward in your own eyes, letting "I don't dare" follow "I want to," like the cat in the old saying that wanted fish but wouldn't get its paws wet?
MACBETH. Enough, please! I dare do everything that is appropriate for a man. Anyone who dares do more is no man at all.

LADY MACBETH. What kind of animal was it, then, that made you reveal this plan to me? When you dared to do it, then you were a man. And to be more than what you were would make you so much more the man. Neither the time nor the place was right then, yet you were willing to create the opportunity. Now time and place have presented themselves, and their very readiness unmakes you. I have nursed a baby and know how tender it is to love the child at my breast. I would have, while it was smiling in my face, torn my nipple from its toothless gums and dashed its brains out, if I had sworn to do so as you have sworn to do this.
MACBETH. If we should fail?

LADY MACBETH. We fail? Just screw your courage to the sticking place, and we won't fail. When Duncan is asleep, which the hard journey of his day will surely invite him to, I will get his two chamberlains so drunk with wine that their memory, the guard of the brain, will turn to fumes, and their reason will become nothing but a distillery. When they lie in a pig-like sleep, their drunken bodies as good as dead, what can't you and I do to the unguarded Duncan? What blame can't we lay on his drunken attendants, who will bear the guilt of our great act?

MACBETH. May you bear only sons! Your fearless spirit should produce nothing but males. Won't everyone believe, when we have smeared the sleeping chamberlains with blood and used their very daggers, that they are the ones who did it?
LADY MACBETH. Who would dare think otherwise, especially when we make our grief and outrage roar loudly at his death?
MACBETH. I am decided, and I commit every fiber of my being to this terrible act. Let us go and deceive everyone with the most pleasant appearance. A false face must hide what the false heart knows.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — Inverness. Court within the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Banquo and Fleance with a torch before him.]
BANQUO. How goes the night, boy?
FLEANCE. The moon has set. I haven't heard the clock.
BANQUO. The moon sets at midnight.
FLEANCE. I think it must be later than that, sir.

BANQUO. Here, take my sword. Heaven is being frugal tonight; all its candles are out. Take this too. A heavy weariness lies on me like lead, and yet I can't sleep. Merciful powers, hold back the cursed thoughts that creep into my mind when I try to rest!
[Enter Macbeth and a Servant with a torch.]
MACBETH. A friend.

BANQUO. What, sir, not in bed yet? The King has gone to sleep. He was in an unusually good mood and sent generous gifts to your servants. He sends this diamond to your wife with his compliments, calling her a most kind hostess, and he has retired in perfect contentment.
MACBETH. We were unprepared, and so our hospitality suffered from our lack of resources, which otherwise would have been more generous.
BANQUO. All was well. I dreamed last night of the three Weird Sisters. They have shown some truth in what they told you.
MACBETH. I don't think about them. Yet when we can find a spare hour, I'd like to spend it discussing that matter, if you're willing to give the time.
BANQUO. Whenever it suits you.
MACBETH. If you stand with me when the time comes, it will bring you honor.
BANQUO. As long as I lose no honor in seeking to gain more, and keep my conscience clear and my loyalty intact, I'll be guided by your counsel.
MACBETH. Good night and rest well.
BANQUO. Thanks, sir. The same to you.
[Exeunt Banquo and Fleance.]
MACBETH. Go tell your mistress to strike the bell when my drink is ready. Then get yourself to bed.
[Exit Servant.]
[A bell rings.]
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Macbeth's Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Lady Macbeth.]

LADY MACBETH. The drink that made them drunk has made me bold. What quenched their fire has lit mine. Listen! Quiet! It was the owl that shrieked, the deadly night watchman who gives the harshest good-night. He is doing it now. The doors are open, and the overfed servants mock their duty with snores. I drugged their bedtime drinks so heavily that death and nature are fighting over them, whether they live or die.
MACBETH. [_Within._] Who's there? Hello!

LADY MACBETH. Oh no! I'm afraid they've woken up, and it isn't done. The attempt without the deed will destroy us. Listen! I laid their daggers ready; he couldn't have missed them. If Duncan hadn't looked so much like my father as he slept, I would have done it myself. My husband!
[Enter Macbeth.]
MACBETH. I have done the deed. Didn't you hear a noise?
LADY MACBETH. I heard the owl scream and the crickets cry. Didn't you speak?
MACBETH. When?
LADY MACBETH. Just now.
MACBETH. As I was coming down?
LADY MACBETH. Yes.
MACBETH. Listen! Who is sleeping in the second chamber?
LADY MACBETH. Donalbain.
MACBETH. This is a terrible sight.
[Looking on his hands.]
LADY MACBETH. What a foolish thing to say, calling it a terrible sight.
MACBETH. One of them laughed in his sleep, and the other cried "Murder!" so that they woke each other up. I stood there and listened. But they said their prayers and went back to sleep.
LADY MACBETH. The two of them are lodged together.
MACBETH. One cried "God bless us!" and the other said "Amen," as if they had seen me with these executioner's hands. Listening to their fear, I could not say "Amen" when they said "God bless us."
LADY MACBETH. Don't think about it so deeply.
MACBETH. But why couldn't I say "Amen"? I needed a blessing more than anyone, and "Amen" stuck in my throat.
LADY MACBETH. We must not dwell on these deeds this way. It will drive us mad.

MACBETH. I thought I heard a voice cry "Sleep no more! Macbeth is murdering sleep!" Innocent sleep. Sleep that knits up the raveled threads of worry. Sleep, the death of each day's life, the bath after hard labor, the balm for wounded minds, nature's great restorative, the chief nourishment at life's feast.
LADY MACBETH. What do you mean?
MACBETH. It kept crying "Sleep no more!" to the whole house: "Glamis has murdered sleep, and therefore Cawdor shall sleep no more. Macbeth shall sleep no more!"

LADY MACBETH. Who was it that cried out like that? Why, worthy lord, you weaken your noble strength by thinking about these things in such a sick way. Go get some water and wash this filthy evidence from your hands. Why did you bring these daggers from the room? They must stay there. Go carry them back and smear the sleeping servants with blood.
MACBETH. I will not go back. I am afraid to think about what I have done. I dare not look at it again.

LADY MACBETH. How weak-willed! Give me the daggers. The sleeping and the dead are nothing more than pictures. It is only a child's eye that is frightened by a painted devil. If Duncan is still bleeding, I'll smear the servants' faces with his blood, because it must look like their guilt.
[Exit. Knocking within.]

MACBETH. Where is that knocking coming from? What is happening to me, when every noise terrifies me? What hands are these? They're plucking out my eyes! Will all the water in the ocean wash this blood clean from my hands? No. These hands of mine would sooner turn the countless seas red, making the green ocean entirely crimson.
[Enter Lady Macbeth.]

LADY MACBETH. My hands are as red as yours, but I would be ashamed to have a heart so white with fear. [_Knocking within._] I hear knocking at the south entrance. Let us go back to our bedroom. A little water will clear us of this deed. How easy that is! Your composure has completely abandoned you. [_Knocking within._] Listen, more knocking. Put on your nightgown, in case we're called and they find us still awake. Don't lose yourself so completely in your thoughts.
MACBETH. Knowing what I've done, I'd rather not know myself. [_Knocking within._] Wake Duncan with your knocking! I wish you could!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — Macbeth's Castle
paragraphs: [Enter a Porter. Knocking within.]

PORTER. There's some knocking indeed! If a man were the porter of hell's gate, he'd get tired of turning the key. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock, knock! Who's there, in the name of the devil? Here's a farmer who hanged himself because he expected prices to drop after a good harvest. Come right in! Better bring plenty of handkerchiefs; you'll sweat in here. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock! Who's there, in the other devil's name? Well now, here's a smooth-talking liar who could swear on both sides of any argument, who committed plenty of treason for God's sake but couldn't talk his way into heaven. Come in, you equivocator! [_Knocking._] Knock, knock, knock! Who's there? Here's an English tailor who's been sent here for skimping on cloth while making French-style trousers. Come in, tailor; here you can heat your pressing iron. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock! Never a moment's peace! Who are you? But this place is too cold for hell. I'll stop playing hell's doorman. I had intended to let in someone from every profession that takes the flowery path to the everlasting bonfire. [_Knocking._] All right, all right! Coming! Please, remember to tip the porter.
[Opens the gate.]
[Enter Macduff and Lennox.]
MACDUFF. Was it so late when you went to bed, friend, that you're having trouble getting up?
PORTER. To tell the truth, sir, we were drinking until the second rooster crowed. And drink, sir, is a great promoter of three things.
MACDUFF. What three things does drink especially promote?

PORTER. Well, sir: a red nose, sleep, and urination. As for lust, sir, it both encourages and discourages it. It creates the desire but takes away the ability. So heavy drinking could be called a double-dealer when it comes to lust: it builds a man up and tears him down; it eggs him on and holds him back; it persuades him and then defeats him; it props him up and then lets him down. In short, it cheats him into a stupor, and having lied to him, leaves him flat.
MACDUFF. I think drink got the better of you last night.
PORTER. That it did, sir, it had me by the throat. But I gave as good as I got. And though it knocked my legs out from under me a few times, I managed to throw it off in the end.
MACDUFF. Is your master up?
[Enter Macbeth.]
LENNOX. Good morning, noble sir!
MACBETH. Good morning, both of you!
MACDUFF. Is the King awake, worthy thane?
MACBETH. Not yet.
MACDUFF. He asked me to call on him early. I've almost missed the hour.
MACBETH. I'll take you to him.
MACDUFF. I know this is a joyful inconvenience for you, but still, it is an inconvenience.
MACBETH. Work we enjoy makes the trouble worthwhile. This is the door.
MACDUFF. I'll be bold enough to knock, since that is my appointed duty.
[Exit Macduff.]
LENNOX. Is the King leaving today?
MACBETH. He is. That was his plan.

LENNOX. The night was wild. Where we were sleeping, our chimneys were blown down. There were strange screams of death heard in the air, and terrible voices prophesying catastrophic events hatched in these dreadful times. The owl shrieked the whole night long. Some say the earth trembled and shook with fever.
MACBETH. It was a rough night.
LENNOX. I'm young, but I can't remember anything like it.
[Enter Macduff.]
MACDUFF. Oh horror, horror, horror! No tongue or heart can conceive or name you!
MACBETH, LENNOX. What's the matter?
MACDUFF. Chaos has created its masterpiece! The most sacrilegious murder has broken into the Lord's anointed temple and stolen the life from it!
MACBETH. What are you saying? The life?
LENNOX. Do you mean His Majesty?
MACDUFF. Go into the chamber and destroy your own sight with a new Gorgon. Don't ask me to speak. See for yourselves, and then speak.
[Exeunt Macbeth and Lennox.]
[Alarum-bell rings.]
[Enter Lady Macbeth.]
LADY MACBETH. What is happening, that such a terrible alarm calls the sleepers of this house to attention? Speak, speak!
MACDUFF. Oh gentle lady, it is not for you to hear what I could say. The words, in a woman's ear, would kill as they fell.
[Enter Banquo.]
LADY MACBETH. Oh no! What, in our house?
BANQUO. Too cruel anywhere. Dear Macduff, I beg you, take it back and say it isn't so.
[Enter Macbeth and Lennox with Ross.]

MACBETH. If I had died an hour before this happened, I would have lived a blessed life. From this moment on, there is nothing worth taking seriously in this mortal world. Everything is a mere toy. Honor and grace are dead. The wine of life has been drained, and nothing but the dregs are left for this world to boast about.
[Enter Malcolm and Donalbain.]
DONALBAIN. What is wrong?
MACBETH. You are what is wrong, and you don't know it yet. The spring, the source, the fountain of your blood has been stopped. The very origin of it has been cut off.
MACDUFF. Your royal father has been murdered.
MALCOLM. Oh! By whom?

LENNOX. It seems his own chamberlains did it. Their hands and faces were smeared with blood. So were their daggers, which we found unwiped on their pillows. They stared blankly, looking deranged. No man's life could be trusted to them.
MACBETH. Yet I do regret my fury in killing them.
MACDUFF. Why did you do that?

MACBETH. Who can be wise, stunned, calm, and furious, loyal and neutral, all at the same time? No one. The urgency of my violent love outran the restraint of reason. There lay Duncan, his silver skin laced with his golden blood, and his gaping wounds looked like a breach in nature for destruction to pour through. There were the murderers, drenched in the colors of their trade, their daggers obscenely coated with gore. Who could have held back, who had a heart capable of love, and courage enough to show it?
LADY MACBETH. Help me away from here!
MACDUFF. Look after the lady.
MALCOLM. Why do we stay silent, we who have the most right to speak on this matter?
DONALBAIN. What should we say here, where our fate, hidden in some small corner, may rush out and seize us? Let's get away. Our tears haven't come yet.
MALCOLM. Nor has our grief found its voice.
BANQUO. Look after the lady!
[Lady Macbeth is carried out.]
MACDUFF. And so do I.
ALL. So do we all.
MACBETH. Let us quickly put on our clothes and armor and meet together in the hall.
ALL. Agreed.
[Exeunt all but Malcolm and Donalbain.]
MALCOLM. What will you do? Let's not stay with them. Showing a grief we don't feel is easy for a dishonest man. I'll go to England.

DONALBAIN. And I'll go to Ireland. We'll be safer apart than together. Wherever we are, there are daggers hidden in men's smiles. The closer someone is to us by blood, the more likely they are to spill ours.

MALCOLM. This murderous arrow that has been shot hasn't landed yet, and our safest course is to get out of its path. So let's ride. Let's not bother with formal goodbyes but slip away. There is justification in fleeing when there is no mercy left to be found.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — Without the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Ross and an Old Man.]
OLD MAN. I can remember seventy years well enough, and in that time I have seen dreadful hours and strange things. But this terrible night has made everything before it seem trivial.

ROSS. You can see, old man, that the heavens themselves are troubled by what man has done and are threatening his bloody stage. By the clock it's daytime, and yet dark night strangles the sun. Is it the night's dominance or the day's shame that buries the face of the earth in darkness when living light should be shining on it?
OLD MAN. It's unnatural, just like the deed that was done. Just last Tuesday, a falcon, soaring at its highest point, was attacked and killed by an ordinary mousing owl.

ROSS. And Duncan's horses, which is the strangest and most certain thing, beautiful and swift, the best of their breed, turned wild, broke out of their stalls, and fought against obedience as if they were making war against mankind.
OLD MAN. It's said they ate each other.
ROSS. They did, to the amazement of my own eyes. Here comes the good Macduff.
[Enter Macduff.]
MACDUFF. Well, don't you see what's happened?
ROSS. Is it known who committed this more than bloody deed?
MACDUFF. The men that Macbeth killed.
ROSS. What a tragedy! What could they have hoped to gain?
MACDUFF. They were bribed. Malcolm and Donalbain, the King's two sons, have stolen away and fled, which throws suspicion of the deed onto them.
ROSS. How unnatural! Wasteful ambition that devours the very thing that sustains your own life! Then it seems most likely that the crown will fall to Macbeth.
MACDUFF. He has already been chosen and has gone to Scone to be crowned.
ROSS. Where is Duncan's body?
MACDUFF. It has been carried to Colmekill, the sacred burial place of his ancestors and guardian of their bones.
ROSS. Will you go to Scone?
MACDUFF. No, cousin, I'll go home to Fife.
ROSS. Well, I will go to Scone.
MACDUFF. Well, I hope things go well there. Goodbye! Let's hope our old robes fit more comfortably than our new ones!
ROSS. Farewell, old man.
OLD MAN. God's blessing go with you, and with all those who would make good out of bad and friends out of foes!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Forres. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter Banquo.]

BANQUO. You have it now: King, Cawdor, Glamis, everything, just as the Weird Women promised. And I fear you played most foully to get it. Yet they also said the crown would not remain with your descendants, and that I myself would be the root and father of many kings. If truth comes from them, as their predictions have proved true for you, Macbeth, why shouldn't their words serve as prophecies for me too, and give me hope? But enough. No more of that.
[Sennet sounded. Enter Macbeth as King, Lady Macbeth as Queen; Lennox, Ross, Lords, and Attendants.]
MACBETH. Here is our chief guest.
LADY MACBETH. If he had been forgotten, it would have been like a gap in our great feast, and entirely unfitting.
MACBETH. We are holding a formal dinner tonight, sir, and I request your presence.
BANQUO. Let Your Highness command me. My duties are bound to you with an unbreakable tie, forever.
MACBETH. Are you riding this afternoon?
BANQUO. Yes, my good lord.
MACBETH. Otherwise, we would have wanted your good advice in today's council, which has always been both serious and profitable. But we'll save it for tomorrow. How far are you riding?
BANQUO. Far enough, my lord, to fill up the time between now and supper. Unless my horse goes faster than expected, I'll have to borrow an hour or two of darkness.
MACBETH. Don't miss our feast.
BANQUO. My lord, I will not.

MACBETH. We hear that our murderous cousins have settled in England and Ireland, not confessing their cruel act of killing their own father, but instead filling people's ears with strange lies. But we'll discuss that tomorrow, when we'll also have matters of state that require both our attention. Hurry to your horse. Goodbye, until you return tonight. Is Fleance going with you?
BANQUO. Yes, my good lord. It's time we were off.
MACBETH. I wish your horses swift and sure. I commend you to their backs. Farewell.
[Exit Banquo.]
[Exeunt Lady Macbeth, Lords, &c.]
SERVANT. They are waiting outside the palace gate, my lord.
MACBETH. Bring them to me.
[Exit Servant.]
[Enter Servant with two Murderers.]
[Exit Servant.]
FIRST MURDERER. It was as you said, Your Highness.

MACBETH. Well then. Have you thought about what I told you? You now know that it was Banquo who held you down in the past, which you had blamed on me, an innocent man. I proved this to you at our last meeting, showing you how you were deceived, who was behind it, who worked against you, and everything else that would tell even a half-wit or a madman: "This was Banquo's doing."
FIRST MURDERER. You made it clear to us.

MACBETH. I did. And now we come to the point of this second meeting. Are you so patient by nature that you can let this go? Are you so saintly that you'd pray for this man and his children, whose heavy hand has bent you down to the grave and beggared your families forever?
FIRST MURDERER. We are men, my lord.

MACBETH. Yes, you pass for men in the general list, just as hounds, greyhounds, mongrels, spaniels, mutts, water dogs, and half-wolves are all called dogs. But the proper catalog distinguishes the fast from the slow, the clever from the dull, the guard dog from the hunter, each one according to the gift that nature gave it, by which it receives its particular rank beyond the common name that lumps them all together. The same goes for men. Now, if you hold a place in the ranks of men that is not the lowest, tell me so, and I will put a task to you whose completion will remove your enemy, bind you to my heart and love, and cure the sickness I suffer as long as Banquo lives. In his death, I would be perfectly well.
SECOND MURDERER. I am one, my lord, whom the cruel blows and insults of the world have made so bitter that I don't care what I do to spite it.
FIRST MURDERER. And I am another, so weary of bad luck and beaten down by fortune that I'd stake my life on any gamble to either fix it or end it.
MACBETH. You both know that Banquo was your enemy.
BOTH MURDERERS. True, my lord.

MACBETH. He is mine too, and so dangerously close to threatening my life that every minute he exists is like a knife at my throat. I could use my naked power as king to simply sweep him from my sight and justify it by royal command. But I must not, because he and I share certain friends whose loyalty I cannot afford to lose. I must publicly mourn the very man I myself have struck down. And that is why I turn to you for help, hiding the business from public view for various important reasons.
SECOND MURDERER. We will do whatever you command, my lord.
FIRST MURDERER. Even if it costs our lives—

MACBETH. Your determination shines through. Within the hour, I will tell you exactly where to position yourselves and the precise moment to strike. It must be done tonight, and at some distance from the palace. Always remember that I must remain completely clear of suspicion. And along with Banquo, his son Fleance, who keeps him company and whose death matters to me no less than his father's, must share the same dark fate. Make up your minds on your own. I'll come to you shortly.
BOTH MURDERERS. We are resolved, my lord.
MACBETH. I'll send for you right away. Wait inside.
[Exeunt Murderers.]
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — Another Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter Lady Macbeth and a Servant.]
LADY MACBETH. Has Banquo left the court?
SERVANT. Yes, madam, but he returns tonight.
LADY MACBETH. Tell the King I would like a few words with him at his convenience.
SERVANT. Yes, madam.
[Exit.]

LADY MACBETH. We have gained nothing and spent everything, when getting what we wanted brings no satisfaction. It is safer to be the one who is destroyed than to live in uncertain joy through destruction.
[Enter Macbeth.]

MACBETH. We have only wounded the snake, not killed it. It will heal and become itself again, while our feeble efforts remain at the mercy of its fangs. But let the whole framework of the world collapse, let both heaven and earth suffer, before we eat our meals in fear and sleep tormented by the terrible dreams that shake us every night. Better to be with the dead, whom we sent to their peace in order to gain ours, than to lie on the rack of the mind in restless agony. Duncan is in his grave. After life's fitful fever, he sleeps well. Treason has done its worst: neither steel, nor poison, nor domestic treachery, nor foreign invasion, nor anything else can touch him now.
LADY MACBETH. Come now, my gentle lord, smooth over your troubled looks. Be bright and cheerful among your guests tonight.

MACBETH. I will, my love, and I ask you to do the same. Pay special attention to Banquo. Honor him with your eyes and your words. We are unsafe for now, and we must wash our reputations in these flattering streams and make our faces masks that hide what our hearts truly feel.
LADY MACBETH. You must stop thinking this way.
MACBETH. Oh, my mind is full of scorpions, dear wife! You know that Banquo and his son Fleance are still alive.
LADY MACBETH. But they won't live forever.

MACBETH. There is comfort in that; they can be gotten to. So be cheerful. Before the bat has flown its dark flight through the cloistered shadows, before the beetle, summoned by dark Hecate, has rung night's drowsy bell with its humming, a deed of dreadful importance will be done.
LADY MACBETH. What is going to be done?

MACBETH. Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest love, until you can applaud the deed. Come, blinding night, blindfold the tender eye of merciful day, and with your bloody and invisible hand cancel and tear to pieces that great bond that keeps me pale with fear! The light thickens, and the crow flies toward the darkening wood. The good things of day begin to fade and drowse, while night's dark agents rouse themselves to hunt their prey. You marvel at my words, but hold still. Things that begin in evil strengthen themselves through more evil. So please, come with me.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — A Park, with a Gate Leading to the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter three Murderers.]
FIRST MURDERER. But who told you to join us?
THIRD MURDERER. Macbeth.
SECOND MURDERER. We don't need to distrust him. He knows our orders and what we're supposed to do, down to the last detail.
FIRST MURDERER. Then stand with us. The west still glimmers with faint streaks of daylight. Now the late traveler spurs his horse to reach the inn in time. The man we're watching for is near.
THIRD MURDERER. Listen! I hear horses.
BANQUO. [_Within._] Give us a light there, ho!
SECOND MURDERER. That must be him. The rest of the expected guests are already inside the court.
FIRST MURDERER. His horses are being led around.
THIRD MURDERER. It's almost a mile, but he usually walks from here to the palace gate, as most people do.
[Enter Banquo and Fleance with a torch.]
SECOND MURDERER. A light, a light!
THIRD MURDERER. It's him.
FIRST MURDERER. Get ready.
BANQUO. It looks like rain tonight.
FIRST MURDERER. Then let it come down!
[Assaults Banquo.]
BANQUO. Oh, treachery! Run, good Fleance, run, run, run! You may avenge me. Oh, you villain!
[Dies. Fleance escapes.]
THIRD MURDERER. Who put out the torch?
FIRST MURDERER. Wasn't that the plan?
THIRD MURDERER. There's only one down. The son has escaped.
SECOND MURDERER. We've botched the most important half of our assignment.
FIRST MURDERER. Well, let's go and report what we did manage to do.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 4 — A Room of State in the Palace
paragraphs: [A banquet prepared. Enter Macbeth, Lady Macbeth, Ross, Lennox, Lords and Attendants.]
MACBETH. You know your own ranks; sit down accordingly. A hearty welcome to all, from first to last.
LORDS. Thanks to Your Majesty.
MACBETH. We will mingle with our guests and play the humble host. Our hostess will stay in her seat of honor, but at the right moment we'll ask her to welcome you.
LADY MACBETH. Say it for me, sir, to all our friends. My heart tells them they are welcome.
[Enter first Murderer to the door.]

MACBETH. See, they return your greeting with heartfelt thanks. Both sides of the table are even. I'll sit here in the middle. Be free and easy, and soon we'll toast a round. [_Goes to the door._] There's blood on your face.
MURDERER. Then it's Banquo's.
MACBETH. Better on your face than inside him. Is he finished?
MURDERER. My lord, his throat is cut. I did that for him.
MACBETH. You are the best of the cutthroats. Yet whoever did the same for Fleance deserves credit too. If you did that, you have no equal.
MURDERER. Most royal sir, Fleance has escaped.

MACBETH. Then my anxiety returns. Otherwise I would have been perfect, as solid as marble, as firmly founded as rock, as free and open as the surrounding air. But now I am hemmed in, confined, imprisoned by nagging doubts and fears. But Banquo is dealt with?
MURDERER. Yes, my good lord. He lies safe in a ditch with twenty deep gashes in his head, the least of which would have killed him.
MACBETH. Thanks for that. There lies the full-grown serpent. The young one that escaped will develop venom in time, but has no fangs for now. Go. We'll talk again tomorrow.
[Exit Murderer.]

LADY MACBETH. My royal lord, you are not playing host. A feast where the host doesn't repeatedly assure his guests they are welcome feels more like a paid meal than a gift. If it's just about eating, better to eat at home. Away from home, the seasoning on the meat is the ceremony and courtesy of the host. Without that, the gathering is nothing.
[The Ghost of Banquo rises, and sits in Macbeth's place.]
MACBETH. Sweet reminder! Now, may good digestion follow appetite, and health follow both!
LENNOX. Would Your Highness be pleased to sit?
MACBETH. We would have all of Scotland's finest gathered under one roof if our honored Banquo were here. I hope it's rudeness that keeps him away rather than some misfortune!
ROSS. His absence, sir, breaks his promise. Would Your Highness honor us by taking your seat?
MACBETH. The table is full.
LENNOX. Here is a place reserved for you, sir.
MACBETH. Where?
LENNOX. Right here, my good lord. What disturbs Your Highness?
MACBETH. Which of you has done this?
LORDS. What, my good lord?
MACBETH. You cannot say I did it. Don't shake your blood-soaked hair at me.
ROSS. Gentlemen, stand up. His Highness is not well.

LADY MACBETH. Sit down, worthy friends. My lord is often like this and has been since his youth. Please, stay seated. The fit is brief. In a moment he will be himself again. If you pay too much attention to him, you'll offend him and make it worse. Eat, and pay him no mind. [_To Macbeth._] Are you a man?
MACBETH. Yes, and a bold one, who dares to look at something that would frighten the devil himself.

LADY MACBETH. What nonsense! This is nothing but a painting created by your fear. This is just like that imaginary dagger you said led you to Duncan. These outbursts and startled reactions, these imitations of true fear, would be fitting for a ghost story told by a woman at the fireside, vouched for by her grandmother. Shame on you! Why do you make such faces? When all is said and done, you are staring at an empty chair.

MACBETH. Please, look there! Look! See! What do you say? Why should I care? If you can nod, then speak too. If our tombs and graves are going to send back the people we bury, then our monuments might as well be the stomachs of vultures.
[Ghost disappears.]
LADY MACBETH. What, has fear made you completely lose your senses?
MACBETH. As sure as I stand here, I saw him.
LADY MACBETH. Shame on you!

MACBETH. Blood has been shed before now, in the old days, before civilized law tamed society. Yes, and since then too, murders have been committed that are too terrible for the ear to hear. The thing is, in the past, when you knocked a man's brains out, he died, and that was the end of it. But now they rise again with twenty fatal wounds on their heads and push us from our seats. That is stranger than the murder itself.
LADY MACBETH. My worthy lord, your noble friends are missing you.

MACBETH. I had forgotten. Don't be alarmed by me, my most worthy friends. I have a strange condition, which is nothing to those who know me well. Come, love and health to all! Then I'll sit down. Give me some wine; fill the cup. I drink to the joy of the entire table, and to our dear friend Banquo, whom we miss. I wish he were here! To all, and to him, we drink. And our duty to all.
[Ghost rises again.]
LORDS. Our duty to you, and we honor the toast.
MACBETH. Get away! Get out of my sight! Let the earth hide you! Your bones are hollow, your blood is cold. There is no power of sight in those eyes you glare with!
LADY MACBETH. Dear guests, think of this as nothing unusual, just a habit. It is nothing more. It only spoils the pleasure of the evening.

MACBETH. Anything a man dares, I dare. Come at me in the form of a rugged Russian bear, an armored rhinoceros, or a Hyrcanian tiger. Take any shape but the one you have, and my nerves will never tremble. Or come alive again and challenge me to a duel in the wilderness. If I tremble then, call me a baby girl's doll. Away, horrible shadow! You unreal mockery, away!
[Ghost disappears.]
LADY MACBETH. You have ruined the good cheer and broken up the pleasant gathering with your extraordinary behavior.

MACBETH. Can such things happen, and just pass over us like a summer cloud, without filling us with special wonder? You make me doubt my own nature when I see that you can look upon such sights and keep the natural color in your cheeks, while mine are white with fear.
ROSS. What sights, my lord?
LADY MACBETH. Please, don't speak to him. He only gets worse. Questions enrage him. Good night at once. Don't worry about leaving in order of rank. Just go, now.
LENNOX. Good night, and may better health attend His Majesty!
LADY MACBETH. A kind good night to all!
[Exeunt all Lords and Attendants.]

MACBETH. Blood will have blood, they say. Stones have been known to move and trees to speak. By omens and hidden connections, by ravens and crows, the most secret murderer has been brought to light. What time of night is it?
LADY MACBETH. It's almost impossible to tell whether it's night or morning.
MACBETH. What do you make of Macduff refusing to come when I summoned him?
LADY MACBETH. Did you actually send for him?

MACBETH. I heard about his refusal indirectly, but I will send a direct summons. There isn't a single lord among them in whose house I don't have a paid informer. I will go tomorrow, and early, to visit the Weird Sisters. They shall tell me more. I am now determined to know the worst by the worst means possible. For my own good, everything else must give way. I am so deep in blood that, if I stopped now, going back would be as hard as going forward. I have strange things in my head that must be acted on before they can be examined too closely.
LADY MACBETH. You need what is the seasoning of all life: sleep.
MACBETH. Come, let's go to sleep. My strange delusion is just the beginner's fear that comes from inexperience. We are still young in this business of crime.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 5 — The Heath
paragraphs: [Thunder. Enter the three Witches meeting Hecate.]
FIRST WITCH. Why, how now, Hecate? You look angry.

HECATE. Don't I have reason to be, you impudent hags? How dare you trade and deal with Macbeth in riddles and matters of death, and I, the mistress of your spells, the secret architect of all harmful magic, was never called to play my part or display the glory of our craft? And what's worse, everything you've done has been for a willful, spiteful, ungrateful man who, like all others, loves only for his own purposes, not for yours. But make it right now. Go, and meet me at the pit of Acheron tomorrow morning. He will come there to learn his destiny. Bring your pots and your spells, your charms and everything else. I'm off through the air. Tonight I'll spend working toward a disastrous and fatal end. Great work must be accomplished before noon. On the tip of the moon there hangs a magical drop, and I'll catch it before it falls to the ground. Distilled by magic arts, it will conjure up illusions so powerful that they'll draw him on to his destruction. He will scorn fate, mock death, and carry his hopes above wisdom, grace, and fear. And as you all know, overconfidence is humanity's greatest enemy.
[Music and song within, "Come away, come away" &c.]
[Exit.]
FIRST WITCH. Come, let's hurry. She'll be back again soon.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 6 — Forres. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter Lennox and another Lord.]

LENNOX. My earlier remarks have only echoed what you were already thinking, and you can draw your own conclusions. I'll only say that things have been strangely managed. The gracious Duncan was pitied by Macbeth, sure, but Duncan was already dead by then. And the brave Banquo walked out too late at night. You might say, if you like, that Fleance killed him, since Fleance ran away. People shouldn't walk so late. And who can help thinking how monstrous it was for Malcolm and Donalbain to kill their own gracious father? A damned act! How it grieved Macbeth! Didn't he, in righteous rage, immediately tear apart the two servants who were slaves to drink and prisoners of sleep? Wasn't that nobly done? And wisely too, because it would have angered anyone to hear those men deny it. So I say Macbeth has handled everything well. And I do think that if he had Duncan's sons in his power, and God willing he won't, they would discover what it means to kill a father. And so would Fleance. But enough of that! I hear that because of his blunt words and his failure to attend the tyrant's feast, Macduff has fallen out of favor. Sir, can you tell me where Macduff has gone?

LORD. The son of Duncan, from whom this tyrant withholds the crown that is rightfully his, lives in the English court and has been received by the most devout King Edward with such grace that misfortune has done nothing to diminish his high standing. Macduff has gone there to beg the holy king for his help in rousing Northumberland and the warlike Siward, so that with their aid and the blessing of heaven, we may once again have food at our tables, sleep through our nights, free our feasts and banquets from bloody knives, give honest loyalty, and receive the honors we all long for. This news has so infuriated the King that he is preparing for war.
LENNOX. Did he send for Macduff?

LORD. He did, and when the messenger received an absolute refusal, the man turned his back on the surly messenger with a disapproving hum, as if to say, "You'll regret the day you gave me this answer."

LENNOX. And that should warn Macduff to keep as much distance as his wisdom can manage. May some holy angel fly to the court of England and deliver his message before he arrives, so that a swift blessing may soon return to our suffering country under its cursed ruler!
LORD. I'll send my prayers with him.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — A Dark Cave. In the Middle, a Cauldron Boiling
paragraphs: [Thunder. Enter the three Witches.]
FIRST WITCH. Three times the striped cat has meowed.
SECOND WITCH. Three times, and once the hedgehog has whined.
THIRD WITCH. My familiar spirit cries: it's time, it's time!

FIRST WITCH. Round about the cauldron go. Into the poisoned brew throw a toad that under a cold stone for thirty-one days and nights has sweated out its venom while sleeping. You boil first in the charmed pot!
ALL. Double, double, toil and trouble. Fire, burn, and cauldron, bubble.

SECOND WITCH. A slice of marshy snake, into the cauldron boil and bake. Eye of newt, and toe of frog, fur of bat, and tongue of dog. Adder's forked tongue, and blind worm's sting, lizard's leg, and owlet's wing, for a spell of powerful trouble, like a hell-broth boil and bubble.
ALL. Double, double, toil and trouble. Fire, burn, and cauldron, bubble.

THIRD WITCH. Scale of dragon, tooth of wolf, dried flesh of a witch, stomach and gullet of a ravenous shark from the salt sea, root of hemlock dug up in the dark, liver of a blasphemer, gall of goat, and slips of yew cut during an eclipse of the moon, nose of a Turk, and a Tartar's lips, finger of an infant strangled at birth and delivered in a ditch by a prostitute. Make the gruel thick and slimy. Add to it a tiger's guts, for the ingredients of our cauldron.
ALL. Double, double, toil and trouble. Fire, burn, and cauldron, bubble.
SECOND WITCH. Cool it with a baboon's blood. Then the charm is firm and good.
[Enter Hecate.]
HECATE. Oh, well done! I applaud your efforts. Everyone shall share in the rewards. And now, dance around the cauldron and sing, like elves and fairies in a ring, enchanting everything you've put in.
[Music and a song: "Black Spirits," &c.]
[Exit Hecate.]
SECOND WITCH. By the pricking of my thumbs, something wicked this way comes. Open, locks, whoever knocks!
[Enter Macbeth.]
MACBETH. Well now, you secret, black, and midnight hags! What are you doing?
ALL. A deed without a name.

MACBETH. I command you, by whatever dark art you practice, however you came to know it, answer me. Even if you unleash the winds and let them fight against the churches, even if the foaming waves swallow up all navigation, even if standing grain is flattened and trees are blown down, even if castles topple onto their guards' heads, even if palaces and pyramids crumble to their foundations, even if the very seeds of all nature tumble together until destruction itself is sick of destroying, answer what I ask you.
FIRST WITCH. Speak.
SECOND WITCH. Ask.
THIRD WITCH. We'll answer.
FIRST WITCH. Would you rather hear it from our mouths, or from our masters?
MACBETH. Call them. Let me see them.
FIRST WITCH. Pour in the blood of a sow that has eaten her nine piglets. Throw in the grease that has dripped from a murderer's gibbet into the flame.
ALL. Come, high or low. Show yourself and your power!
[Thunder. An Apparition of an armed Head rises.]
MACBETH. Tell me, you unknown power—
FIRST WITCH. He knows your thoughts. Hear what he says, but do not speak.
APPARITION. Macbeth! Macbeth! Macbeth! Beware Macduff. Beware the Thane of Fife. Dismiss me. Enough.
[Descends.]
MACBETH. Whatever you are, thank you for your warning. You have struck the exact note of my fear. But one more word—
FIRST WITCH. He will not be commanded. Here is another, more powerful than the first.
[Thunder. An Apparition of a bloody Child rises.]
APPARITION. Macbeth! Macbeth! Macbeth!
MACBETH. If I had three ears, I'd listen with all of them.
APPARITION. Be bloody, bold, and resolute. Laugh with contempt at the power of any man, for no one born of a woman shall ever harm Macbeth.
[Descends.]

MACBETH. Then live, Macduff. Why should I fear you? But still, I'll make doubly sure and take an extra guarantee from fate. You shall not live, so that I can tell my pale-hearted fear it's a liar and sleep soundly despite any thunder.
[Thunder. An Apparition of a Child crowned, with a tree in his hand, rises.]
ALL. Listen, but do not speak to it.

APPARITION. Be lion-hearted, proud, and take no care about who is angry, who complains, or where conspirators are. Macbeth shall never be defeated until Great Birnam Wood marches to high Dunsinane Hill to fight against him.
[Descends.]

MACBETH. That will never happen. Who can command a forest? Who can order a tree to pull up its earth-bound roots? Sweet prophecies! Wonderful! Rebellion, never raise your head until the wood of Birnam rises and moves. And our well-placed Macbeth shall live out his natural life and die of old age like everyone else. Yet my heart aches to know one thing more. Tell me, if your art can tell this much: will Banquo's descendants ever reign in this kingdom?
ALL. Seek to know no more.
MACBETH. I will have an answer. Deny me this, and an eternal curse fall on you! Let me know. Why is the cauldron sinking? And what is that sound?
[Hautboys.]
FIRST WITCH. Show!
SECOND WITCH. Show!
THIRD WITCH. Show!
ALL. Show his eyes and grieve his heart. Come like shadows, and so depart!
[A show of eight kings appear, and pass over in order, the last with a glass in his hand; Banquo following.]

MACBETH. You look too much like the spirit of Banquo. Get down! Your crown burns my eyeballs. And you, with your other gold-bound brow, you look like the first. A third looks just like the previous ones. Filthy hags! Why do you show me this? A fourth! My eyes, will they burst? What, will the line stretch out to the end of time? Another! A seventh! I'll see no more. And yet the eighth appears, holding a mirror that shows me many more. Some I see carrying double orbs and triple scepters. Horrible sight! Now I see it is true, for the blood-clotted Banquo smiles at me and points at them as his descendants. What! Is this really so?

FIRST WITCH. Yes, sir, all this is so. But why does Macbeth stand here so amazed? Come, sisters, let us cheer his spirits and show him the best of our entertainment. I'll charm the air to make music while you perform your wild dance, so that this great king may graciously say we did our duty to welcome him.
[Music. The Witches dance, and vanish.]
MACBETH. Where are they? Gone? Let this cursed hour stand marked in the calendar forever! Come in, whoever is outside!
[Enter Lennox.]
LENNOX. What is Your Grace's wish?
MACBETH. Did you see the Weird Sisters?
LENNOX. No, my lord.
MACBETH. Didn't they come past you?
LENNOX. No, indeed, my lord.
MACBETH. May the air they ride on be infected, and damn every soul that trusts them! I heard the galloping of horses. Who was it that passed by?
LENNOX. Two or three men, my lord, who bring word that Macduff has fled to England.
MACBETH. Fled to England!
LENNOX. Yes, my good lord.

MACBETH. Time, you have beaten me to the punch. Intentions that aren't acted on immediately are never carried out. From this moment forward, the first impulses of my heart shall become the first actions of my hand. And right now, to turn my thoughts into deeds immediately: I will attack Macduff's castle, seize Fife, and put to the sword his wife, his children, and every unfortunate soul connected to him. No more foolish boasting. This deed I'll do before this anger cools. But no more visions! Where are those men? Come, take me to them.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Fife. A Room in Macduff's Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Lady Macduff her Son and Ross.]
LADY MACDUFF. What had he done to make him flee the country?
ROSS. You must be patient, madam.
LADY MACDUFF. He had no patience himself. His flight was madness. When our actions don't make us traitors, our fears do.
ROSS. You don't know whether it was wisdom or fear that made him go.

LADY MACDUFF. Wisdom! To leave his wife, to leave his children, his home and his titles, in a place he himself runs from? He doesn't love us. He lacks the natural instinct that even the wren, the smallest of birds, has, fighting to protect her young ones in the nest against the owl. It's all fear and no love. And there's no wisdom either when the flight runs against all reason.

ROSS. My dearest cousin, please, control yourself. As for your husband, he is noble, wise, and judicious, and knows best what these dangerous times demand. I don't dare say much more. But the times are cruel when we are called traitors without knowing why, when we cling to rumors of what we fear without knowing what it is we actually fear, and float on a wild and violent sea, tossed in every direction. I must take my leave of you. It won't be long before I'm back again. Things at their worst will either stop or climb back up to what they were before. My pretty cousin, blessings upon you!
LADY MACDUFF. He has a father, and yet he's fatherless.
ROSS. I am such a fool that if I stay any longer, I'll embarrass myself and upset you. I'll take my leave at once.
[Exit.]
LADY MACDUFF. Son, your father is dead. What will you do now? How will you live?
SON. As birds do, Mother.
LADY MACDUFF. What, on worms and flies?
SON. On whatever I can find, I mean. That's what they do.
LADY MACDUFF. Poor little bird! You'd never worry about nets or birdlime, traps or snares.
SON. Why should I, Mother? Those aren't set for poor birds. My father is not dead, no matter what you say.
LADY MACDUFF. Yes, he is dead. How will you manage without a father?
SON. Well, how will you manage without a husband?
LADY MACDUFF. I can buy myself twenty husbands at any market.
SON. Then you'd buy them just to sell them again.
LADY MACDUFF. You speak with all the cleverness you have, and yet it's clever enough for your age.
SON. Was my father a traitor, Mother?
LADY MACDUFF. Yes, he was.
SON. What is a traitor?
LADY MACDUFF. Someone who makes promises and breaks them.
SON. And is everyone who does that a traitor?
LADY MACDUFF. Everyone who does that is a traitor and must be hanged.
SON. And must everyone who makes promises and breaks them be hanged?
LADY MACDUFF. Every one.
SON. Who would hang them?
LADY MACDUFF. The honest men.
SON. Then the liars and promise-breakers are fools, because there are enough of them to beat the honest men and hang them instead.
LADY MACDUFF. God help you, poor little monkey! But how will you do without a father?
SON. If he were dead, you'd weep for him. If you didn't weep, it would be a good sign that I'd soon have a new father.
LADY MACDUFF. Poor chatterbox, how you talk!
[Enter a Messenger.]

MESSENGER. God bless you, madam! I am not known to you, but I know well your honorable standing. I fear some danger is approaching you quickly. If you will take a humble man's advice, do not be found here. Leave at once with your little ones. I know this warning itself is frightening, but to do nothing would be a cruelty even worse, and that cruelty is already too close to you. Heaven preserve you! I dare not stay any longer.
[Exit.]

LADY MACDUFF. Where should I run? I have done nothing wrong. But I remember now that I am in this earthly world, where doing harm is often praised and doing good is sometimes considered dangerous foolishness. Why, then, do I put up the womanly defense of saying I have done no harm? What are these faces?
[Enter Murderers.]
FIRST MURDERER. Where is your husband?
LADY MACDUFF. In no place so unholy that the likes of you would find him there, I hope.
FIRST MURDERER. He's a traitor.
SON. You lie, you shaggy-eared villain!
FIRST MURDERER. What, you little egg!
[Stabbing him.]
SON. He has killed me, Mother! Run away, I beg you!
[Dies. Exit Lady Macduff, crying "Murder!" and pursued by the Murderers.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — England. Before the King's Palace
paragraphs: [Enter Malcolm and Macduff.]
MALCOLM. Let us find some lonely place in the shade and weep until our sorrowful hearts are empty.

MACDUFF. Let us instead take up the deadly sword and, like good men, defend our fallen homeland. Each new morning, new widows cry, new orphans weep, new sorrows strike the face of heaven so that it echoes back as if it shared Scotland's pain, screaming in a voice of grief.

MALCOLM. What I believe, I'll mourn. What I know for certain, I'll believe. And what I can set right, I will, when I find time is on my side. What you've said may well be true. This tyrant, whose very name blisters our tongues, was once thought honest. You loved him once, and he hasn't touched you yet. I am young, but perhaps you hope to gain something from him through me. And it might seem wise to sacrifice a weak, poor, innocent lamb to appease an angry god.
MACDUFF. I am not treacherous.

MALCOLM. But Macbeth is. A good and virtuous nature may give way under the pressure of a royal command. But I ask your pardon. What you are, my suspicions cannot change. Angels are still bright even though the brightest angel fell. Even though everything foul tries to wear the face of grace, grace must still look like itself.
MACDUFF. I have lost my hopes.

MALCOLM. Perhaps right where I found my doubts. Why did you leave your wife and children, those precious bonds of love, so suddenly and without saying goodbye? Please, don't let my suspicions dishonor you. They are for my own safety. You may be perfectly just, whatever I may think.

MACDUFF. Bleed, bleed, poor country! Great tyranny, plant yourself firmly, for goodness does not dare to challenge you. Enjoy your stolen power. Your claim to the throne is secured. Farewell, my lord. I would not be the villain you think I am for all the territory in the tyrant's grip, and all the riches of the East besides.

MALCOLM. Don't be offended. I don't speak from absolute distrust of you. I know our country is sinking under the tyrant's yoke. It weeps, it bleeds, and each new day a fresh wound is added. I know there would be men willing to fight for my cause, and here in generous England I've been offered thousands of good soldiers. But despite all that, when I step on the tyrant's head or wear it on my sword, my poor country will suffer more and in more ways than ever, at the hands of the one who succeeds him.
MACDUFF. Who would that be?

MALCOLM. I mean myself. I know that every kind of vice is so deeply rooted in me that when they are exposed, the black Macbeth will seem as pure as snow, and poor Scotland will consider him a lamb compared to my boundless capacity for harm.
MACDUFF. Not in all the legions of terrible hell can there be found a devil more damned in wickedness than Macbeth.

MALCOLM. I grant you he is bloody, lustful, greedy, false, deceitful, violent, malicious, and guilty of every sin that has a name. But there is no bottom, no limit, to my lust. Your wives, your daughters, your matrons, and your maids could not fill up the well of my desire. My appetite would overwhelm every obstacle in its path. Macbeth would be better as king than someone like me.

MACDUFF. Unbounded excess in one's nature is a kind of tyranny. It has caused the premature downfall of many kings. But don't let that prevent you from claiming what is yours. You can satisfy your desires in plenty and still appear virtuous. You can fool the world easily enough. We have willing women in abundance. The appetite in you cannot be so great that it would consume all those who would offer themselves to greatness.

MALCOLM. Along with that, there grows in my badly composed character such a bottomless greed that, if I were king, I would seize the nobles' lands, steal one man's jewels, another man's house. And the more I had, the hungrier I would become, so that I would invent unjust quarrels against the good and loyal and destroy them for their wealth.

MACDUFF. This greed runs deeper and has more dangerous roots than lust, which passes like summer. It has been the downfall of our murdered kings. Yet don't be afraid. Scotland has enough wealth to satisfy your desires from your own royal holdings alone. All these faults are bearable when weighed against your other virtues.

MALCOLM. But I have no virtues. The qualities that befit a king, such as justice, truthfulness, self-control, stability, generosity, perseverance, mercy, humility, devotion, patience, courage, and fortitude, I have no trace of any of them. Instead, I overflow with every kind of crime, practicing them in every possible way. If I had power, I would pour the sweet milk of harmony into hell, throw the universal peace into chaos, and destroy all unity on earth.
MACDUFF. Oh Scotland, Scotland!
MALCOLM. If such a person is fit to govern, speak. I am as I have described myself.

MACDUFF. Fit to govern? Not fit to live! Oh miserable nation, ruled by a bloody tyrant with no rightful claim to the scepter, when will you see healthy days again, since the truest heir to the throne has accused himself and cursed his own bloodline? Your royal father was a most saintly king. The queen who bore you spent more time on her knees in prayer than on her feet, and died more devoutly with each passing day. Farewell! The evils you have laid upon yourself have banished me from Scotland. Oh, my heart! All my hope ends here.

MALCOLM. Macduff, this noble outburst, born of integrity, has wiped the dark suspicions from my soul and reconciled my thoughts to your good truth and honor. The devilish Macbeth has tried many tricks to lure me into his power, and sensible caution has kept me from rushing to trust too quickly. But God above will judge between you and me! For right now, I take back everything I said against myself. I renounce the stains and accusations I laid upon my own character, for they are foreign to my nature. I am still unknown to women, have never broken an oath, have scarcely desired what was already mine, have never betrayed my word, would not hand over even the devil to his fellow, and take no less delight in truth than in life itself. The first lie I ever told was the one I just told about myself. What I truly am belongs to you and to my poor country. In fact, before you arrived here, old Siward, with ten thousand battle-ready men, was already setting out. Now we'll march together, and may our chances of success match the justice of our cause! Why are you silent?
MACDUFF. Such welcome and unwelcome news at the same time is hard to take in all at once.
[Enter a Doctor.]
MALCOLM. We'll speak more soon. Is the King coming out, I ask you?

DOCTOR. Yes, sir. There is a crowd of miserable souls waiting for his healing touch. Their disease defeats the greatest efforts of medicine, but at his touch, with the holiness heaven has given his hand, they are immediately cured.
MALCOLM. Thank you, doctor.
[Exit Doctor.]
MACDUFF. What disease does he mean?

MALCOLM. It's called the King's Evil, a most miraculous power in this good king. Since I've been staying in England, I've seen him do it often. How he appeals to heaven, he himself knows best, but strangely afflicted people, all swollen and covered with sores, pitiful to look at, beyond the hope of surgery, he cures by hanging a golden coin around their necks, placed there with holy prayers. And it's said that he passes this healing gift down to the kings who follow him. Along with this strange power, he has a heavenly gift of prophecy, and many blessings surround his throne that declare him full of grace.
[Enter Ross.]
MACDUFF. See who comes here?
MALCOLM. A countryman of ours, but I don't recognize him yet.
MACDUFF. My dear and gentle cousin, welcome!
MALCOLM. I recognize him now. Good God, quickly remove whatever keeps us strangers to each other!
ROSS. Amen, sir.
MACDUFF. Does Scotland stand where it did?

ROSS. Alas, poor country! It's almost too afraid to recognize itself. It can no longer be called our mother, but our grave, where no one who knows anything ever smiles, where sighs and groans and shrieks that tear the air are heard so often they go unnoticed, where violent sorrow seems like an everyday event. The funeral bell rings so constantly that no one even asks who has died, and good men's lives expire before the flowers in their caps, dying before they even fall ill.
MACDUFF. Oh, a report too painfully detailed, and yet too true!
MALCOLM. What is the latest grief?
ROSS. News that's even an hour old is already stale. Every minute produces a new one.
MACDUFF. How is my wife?
ROSS. She's well.
MACDUFF. And all my children?
ROSS. Well too.
MACDUFF. The tyrant hasn't disturbed their peace?
ROSS. No, they were at peace when I left them.
MACDUFF. Don't be stingy with your words. How are things?

ROSS. When I came here to bring the news I've carried with a heavy heart, there was a rumor that many worthy men had taken up arms against Macbeth. I believed it all the more readily because I saw the tyrant's army on the march. Now is the time for action. Your presence in Scotland would rally soldiers and even make our women fight to throw off their terrible suffering.
MALCOLM. Let them take comfort that we are coming. Gracious England has lent us good Siward and ten thousand men. There is no older or better soldier in all of Christendom.
ROSS. I wish I could answer this comforting news with the same! But I have words that should be howled into the empty desert air, where no one could hear them.
MACDUFF. What do they concern? The general cause? Or is it a personal grief belonging to a single heart?
