ROSS. There is no honest mind that doesn't share some of this sorrow, though the main part of it belongs to you alone.
MACDUFF. If it's mine, don't keep it from me. Let me have it quickly.
ROSS. Don't let your ears hate my tongue forever for making them hear the heaviest sound they have ever heard.
MACDUFF. I can guess what it is.
ROSS. Your castle was attacked. Your wife and children were savagely slaughtered. To describe the details would be to add your death to the pile of murdered innocents.
MALCOLM. Merciful heaven! What, man, don't pull your hat down over your eyes. Give your sorrow words. The grief that doesn't speak whispers to the overburdened heart and tells it to break.
MACDUFF. My children too?
ROSS. Wife, children, servants, everyone who could be found.
MACDUFF. And I had to be away! My wife killed too?
ROSS. I have said it.
MALCOLM. Take comfort. Let us make medicines of our great revenge to cure this deadly grief.
MACDUFF. He has no children. All my pretty ones? Did you say all? Oh, hell-kite! All? What, all my pretty chickens and their mother, at one terrible swoop?
MALCOLM. Fight your grief like a man.

MACDUFF. I will. But I must also feel it as a man. I cannot help remembering that such precious things once belonged to me. Did heaven look on and would not take their side? Sinful Macduff, they were all struck down because of you! Worthless as I am, the slaughter fell not for their own sins, but for mine. May heaven give them rest now!
MALCOLM. Let this be the whetstone for your sword. Let grief turn to anger. Don't blunt your heart; sharpen it with rage.

MACDUFF. Oh, I could weep like a woman and boast with empty words! But, gentle heavens, cut short all delay. Bring this monster of Scotland face to face with me. Set him within my sword's reach. If he escapes, may heaven forgive him too!

MALCOLM. Now that sounds like a man. Come, let us go to the King. Our army is ready. All we need is the King's permission to depart. Macbeth is ripe for the shaking, and the powers above are preparing their instruments. Take what comfort you can. The night is long that never finds the day.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Dunsinane. A Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter a Doctor of Physic and a Waiting-Gentlewoman.]
DOCTOR. I have watched with you for two nights now, but I can find no truth in your report. When did she last walk in her sleep?

GENTLEWOMAN. Since His Majesty went to war, I have seen her rise from her bed, throw on her nightgown, unlock her writing desk, take out paper, fold it, write on it, read what she wrote, seal it, and return to bed, all while in the deepest sleep.

DOCTOR. A great disturbance of nature, to receive the benefit of sleep while performing the actions of someone awake. In this sleepwalking state, besides the walking and other physical activities, what have you heard her say?
GENTLEWOMAN. Things, sir, that I will not repeat.
DOCTOR. You may tell me, and you really should.
GENTLEWOMAN. Neither to you nor to anyone, since I have no witness to confirm what I heard.
[Enter Lady Macbeth with a taper.]
DOCTOR. How did she get that candle?
GENTLEWOMAN. It was beside her bed. She keeps a light burning beside her constantly. Those are her orders.
DOCTOR. You see, her eyes are open.
GENTLEWOMAN. Yes, but they see nothing.
DOCTOR. What is she doing now? Look how she rubs her hands.
GENTLEWOMAN. That is something she does habitually, as if she is washing her hands. I have seen her continue doing it for a quarter of an hour.
LADY MACBETH. Yet here's a spot.
DOCTOR. Listen, she speaks. I will write down what she says, to fix it more firmly in my memory.

LADY MACBETH. Out, damned spot! Out, I say! One, two. Well then, it's time to do it. Hell is dark! Shame on you, my lord, shame! A soldier, and afraid? What do we need to fear when no one can hold us accountable? Yet who would have thought the old man had so much blood in him?
DOCTOR. Did you hear that?
LADY MACBETH. The Thane of Fife had a wife. Where is she now? What, will these hands never be clean? No more of that, my lord, no more of that. You ruin everything with this nervous flinching.
DOCTOR. Well, well, well. You have come to know things you should not have known.
GENTLEWOMAN. She has said things she should not have said, I am sure of that. Heaven knows what she has known.
LADY MACBETH. The smell of blood is still here. All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand. Oh, oh, oh!
DOCTOR. What a sigh that was! Her heart is terribly burdened.
GENTLEWOMAN. I would not want such a heart in my chest, not for all the dignity in the world.
DOCTOR. Well, well, well.
GENTLEWOMAN. Pray God it will be well, sir.
DOCTOR. This disease is beyond my medical skill. Yet I have known sleepwalkers who have died peacefully in their beds.
LADY MACBETH. Wash your hands. Put on your nightgown. Don't look so pale. I tell you again, Banquo is buried. He cannot come out of his grave.
DOCTOR. Is that so?
LADY MACBETH. To bed, to bed! There's knocking at the gate. Come, come, come, come, give me your hand. What's done cannot be undone. To bed, to bed, to bed!
[Exit.]
DOCTOR. Will she go to bed now?
GENTLEWOMAN. Directly.

DOCTOR. Foul rumors are spreading everywhere. Unnatural deeds breed unnatural troubles. Infected minds will unburden their secrets to their deaf pillows. She needs a priest more than a physician. God, God, forgive us all! Watch over her. Remove anything she could use to harm herself, and keep your eyes on her at all times. So, good night. She has staggered my mind and amazed my sight. I think much, but dare not speak.
GENTLEWOMAN. Good night, good doctor.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — The Country near Dunsinane
paragraphs: [Enter, with drum and colours Menteith, Caithness, Angus, Lennox and Soldiers.]

MENTEITH. The English army is near, led by Malcolm, his uncle Siward, and the good Macduff. They burn for revenge. Their deeply personal causes would stir even a dead man to rise and fight at the bleeding and grim call to arms.
ANGUS. We should meet them near Birnam Wood. That's the direction they're coming from.
CAITHNESS. Does anyone know if Donalbain is with his brother?
LENNOX. He is definitely not. I have a list of all the nobility. Siward's son is there, and many young men barely old enough to call themselves men, now fighting in their first campaign.
MENTEITH. What is the tyrant doing?

CAITHNESS. He is heavily fortifying Great Dunsinane. Some say he's gone mad. Others, who hate him less, call it a courageous fury. But one thing is certain: he can no longer hold his disintegrating cause together with any kind of discipline.

ANGUS. Now he feels his secret murders clinging to his hands. Now, every minute, new revolts condemn his broken faith. Those he commands obey only because they are ordered to, not out of love. Now he feels his title hanging loose around him, like a giant's robe draped on a dwarfish thief.
MENTEITH. Who can blame his tortured nerves for recoiling and startling, when everything inside him condemns itself for being there?
CAITHNESS. Well, let us march on, to give our obedience where it is truly owed. Let us join Malcolm, the medicine for our sick nation, and pour out every drop of our blood in our country's cause.
LENNOX. Or as much as is needed to water the rightful ruler and drown the weeds. Let's march toward Birnam.
[Exeunt, marching.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — Dunsinane. A Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Macbeth, Doctor and Attendants.]

MACBETH. Bring me no more reports. Let them all desert me. Until Birnam Wood moves to Dunsinane, I cannot be touched by fear. What is the boy Malcolm to me? Wasn't he born of a woman? The spirits who know all earthly outcomes have told me this: "Fear not, Macbeth. No man born of a woman shall ever have power over you." Then flee, you treacherous thanes, and go join the soft English. The mind that rules me and the heart I carry shall never sag with doubt or shake with fear.
[Enter a Servant.]
SERVANT. There are ten thousand—
MACBETH. Geese, you fool?
SERVANT. Soldiers, sir.

MACBETH. Go scratch your face and make it red to cover your cowardice, you lily-livered boy. What soldiers, you clown? Death take your soul! Those white cheeks of yours are advertisements for fear. What soldiers, you milk-face?
SERVANT. The English army, if it please you.
MACBETH. Get your face out of my sight.
[Exit Servant.]
[Enter Seyton.]
SEYTON. What is Your Grace's pleasure?
MACBETH. What more news?
SEYTON. Everything that was reported has been confirmed, my lord.
MACBETH. I'll fight until they hack the flesh from my bones. Give me my armor.
SEYTON. It's not needed yet.
MACBETH. I'll put it on anyway. Send out more riders. Scour the countryside. Hang anyone who talks of fear. Give me my armor. How is your patient, Doctor?
DOCTOR. Not so much physically ill, my lord, as she is troubled by thick-coming fantasies that keep her from resting.

MACBETH. Cure her of that. Can't you treat a diseased mind? Pull from her memory a rooted sorrow? Erase the troubles written on her brain? Use some sweet medicine of forgetfulness to cleanse the burdened heart of the dangerous weight that presses upon it?
DOCTOR. In that matter, the patient must cure herself.

MACBETH. Throw medicine to the dogs then; I'll have none of it. Come, put on my armor. Give me my staff. Seyton, send out the riders. Doctor, the thanes are deserting me. Come, sir, hurry. If you could, Doctor, diagnose the disease of my country, find what ails it, and purge it back to sound and pure health, I would applaud you until the echo applauded in return. Pull it off, I say. What drug, what laxative, what purge would flush these English out of here? Have you heard anything about them?
DOCTOR. Yes, my good lord. Your royal preparations for battle have reached our ears.
MACBETH. Bring my armor after me. I will not be afraid of death and ruin until Birnam Forest comes to Dunsinane.
[Exeunt all except Doctor.]
DOCTOR. If I could get away from Dunsinane, no amount of profit would lure me back here.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — Country near Dunsinane. A Wood in View
paragraphs: [Enter, with drum and colours Malcolm, old Siward and his Son, Macduff, Menteith, Caithness, Angus, Lennox, Ross and Soldiers, marching.]
MALCOLM. Cousins, I hope the days are near when we'll be safe in our own homes again.
MENTEITH. We don't doubt it.
SIWARD. What wood is this ahead of us?
MENTEITH. The wood of Birnam.
MALCOLM. Let every soldier cut down a branch and carry it in front of him. That way we'll hide our numbers and make the enemy's scouts report incorrectly.
SOLDIERS. It shall be done.
SIWARD. We've heard nothing new except that the overconfident tyrant is still holed up in Dunsinane and will try to withstand our siege.

MALCOLM. That is his main hope. For whenever men have had a chance to leave him, both the great and the small have deserted, and no one serves him now except men who are forced to, whose hearts are not in it.
MACDUFF. Let our fair judgments wait for the actual outcome. Let us simply be good soldiers and do our duty.

SIWARD. The time is coming that will settle with certainty what we truly have and what we owe. Speculation offers uncertain hopes, but the sure result must be decided by blows in battle. Forward, march to the war.
[Exeunt, marching.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 5 — Dunsinane. Within the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter with drum and colours, Macbeth, Seyton and Soldiers.]

MACBETH. Hang our banners on the outer walls! The cry is still "They come!" Our castle is strong enough to laugh a siege to scorn. Let them sit here until famine and disease eat them away. If they hadn't been reinforced by men who should have been on our side, we could have met them boldly, face to face, and beaten them back home.
[A cry of women within.]
SEYTON. It is the cry of women, my good lord.
[Exit.]

MACBETH. I have almost forgotten what fear tastes like. There was a time when a shriek in the night would have chilled my blood, and a terrifying story would have made the hair on my skin stand up as if it were alive. I have feasted so fully on horrors that dreadful things, familiar to my murderous thoughts, can no longer make me flinch.
[Enter Seyton.]
SEYTON. The Queen, my lord, is dead.

MACBETH. She would have died eventually. There would have been a time for such news. Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow creeps along at this petty pace from day to day, to the last syllable of recorded time. And all our yesterdays have only lit the way for fools toward dusty death. Out, out, brief candle! Life is nothing but a walking shadow, a poor actor who struts and frets his hour upon the stage and then is heard no more. It is a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing.
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. Gracious my lord, I should report what I am certain I saw, but I don't know how to say it.
MACBETH. Well, say it, sir.
MESSENGER. As I stood on watch upon the hill, I looked toward Birnam, and I thought I saw the wood begin to move.
MACBETH. Liar and slave!
MESSENGER. Let me suffer your anger if it isn't true. Within three miles you can see it coming. I tell you, it is a moving forest.

MACBETH. If you're lying, I'll hang you alive from the nearest tree until you starve to death. If what you say is true, you may do the same to me. My resolve is weakening, and I begin to doubt the double-dealing of the fiend that lies like truth: "Fear not, till Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane," and now a wood is coming toward Dunsinane. To arms, to arms, and out! If what this man claims is true, there is no point in fleeing and no point in staying. I am beginning to grow weary of the sun and wish the whole world would fall apart. Ring the alarm bell! Blow, wind! Come, destruction! At least we'll die with our armor on.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 6 — A Plain before the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter, with drum and colours, Malcolm, old Siward, Macduff and their Army, with boughs.]

MALCOLM. We are close enough now. Throw down your leafy camouflage and show yourselves as you truly are. You, worthy uncle, with my cousin, your noble son, shall lead the first charge. Worthy Macduff and I will handle whatever else remains to be done, according to our plan.
SIWARD. Farewell. If we find the tyrant's forces tonight, let us be beaten only if we cannot fight.
MACDUFF. Sound all our trumpets! Give them all the breath they have, those loud heralds of blood and death.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 7 — Another Part of the Plain
paragraphs: [Alarums. Enter Macbeth.]

MACBETH. They have tied me to a stake. I cannot run, but like a bear I must fight each round. Who is there that was not born of a woman? That is the only kind of man I need to fear, and there is none.
[Enter young Siward.]
YOUNG SIWARD. What is your name?
MACBETH. You'll be afraid to hear it.
YOUNG SIWARD. No, even if you called yourself a name more terrible than any in hell.
MACBETH. My name is Macbeth.
YOUNG SIWARD. The devil himself could not speak a name more hateful to my ears.
MACBETH. Nor one more terrifying.
YOUNG SIWARD. You lie, you despicable tyrant! With my sword, I'll prove you a liar.
[They fight, and young Siward is slain.]
MACBETH. You were born of a woman. I smile at swords and laugh at any weapons wielded by a man born of a woman.
[Exit.]
[Alarums. Enter Macduff.]

MACDUFF. The noise of battle is that way. Tyrant, show your face! If you are killed by anyone other than me, the ghosts of my wife and children will haunt me forever. I cannot waste my blows on hired mercenaries whose arms are paid to carry spears. Either you, Macbeth, or else my sword, with its edge still unused, I'll put back in its sheath without having done its work. You should be nearby. By this great racket, someone of great importance seems to be fighting. Let me find him, Fortune, and I ask nothing more.
[Exit. Alarums.]
[Enter Malcolm and old Siward.]

SIWARD. This way, my lord. The castle has surrendered without a fight. The tyrant's men are fighting on both sides. The noble thanes are fighting bravely. The day almost declares itself yours, and there is little left to do.
MALCOLM. We have encountered enemies who are deliberately missing us with their blows.
SIWARD. Enter the castle, sir.
[Exeunt. Alarums.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 8 — Another Part of the Field
paragraphs: [Enter Macbeth.]
MACBETH. Why should I play the Roman fool and fall on my own sword? As long as I see living enemies, my blade does better work on them.
[Enter Macduff.]
MACDUFF. Turn around, you hellhound, turn!
MACBETH. Of all men, I have avoided you. But go back. My soul is already too heavy with your family's blood.
MACDUFF. I have no words. My voice is in my sword, you villain bloodier than words can express!
[They fight.]

MACBETH. You waste your effort. You might as easily cut the uncuttable air with your keen sword as make me bleed. Swing your blade at vulnerable targets. I bear a charmed life that cannot yield to anyone born of a woman.
MACDUFF. Then abandon your charm and know this: Macduff was ripped from his mother's womb before his time. He was not born in the natural way.

MACBETH. Curse the tongue that tells me this, for it has broken the best part of my manhood! And let these cheating demons never be trusted again, who deceive us with double meanings, who keep their word to our ears but break their promise to our hopes! I will not fight you.

MACDUFF. Then surrender, coward, and live to be the spectacle and laughingstock of the age. We'll put you on display like one of our rarest freaks, painted on a pole with a sign underneath that reads: "Here you may see the tyrant."

MACBETH. I will not surrender, to kiss the ground before young Malcolm's feet and be taunted by the jeering mob. Though Birnam Wood has come to Dunsinane, and you stand against me as a man not born of woman, I will fight to the end. I throw my shield before my body. Come on, Macduff, and damn the man who first cries "Stop, enough!"
[Exeunt fighting. Alarums.]
[Retreat. Flourish. Enter, with drum and colours, Malcolm, old Siward, Ross, Thanes and Soldiers.]
MALCOLM. I wish the friends we miss had arrived safely.
SIWARD. Some had to die. And yet, by the men I see here, so great a day as this was won at a small cost.
MALCOLM. Macduff is missing, and your noble son.

ROSS. Your son, my lord, has paid a soldier's debt. He only lived until he proved himself a man. As soon as his bravery confirmed his manhood in the place where he stood and fought without flinching, he died like a man.
SIWARD. Then he is dead?
ROSS. Yes, and carried from the field. Your sorrow must not be measured by his worth, for then it would have no end.
SIWARD. Were his wounds on the front of his body?
ROSS. Yes, on the front.
SIWARD. Then let him be God's soldier! If I had as many sons as I have hairs on my head, I could not wish them a finer death. And so his funeral bell is tolled.
MALCOLM. He deserves more sorrow than that, and I'll give it to him.
SIWARD. He deserves no more. They say he fought well and settled his account. And so, God be with him! Here comes fresher comfort.
[Enter Macduff with Macbeth's head.]

MACDUFF. Hail, King! For that is what you are. Look, here stands the usurper's cursed head. The time is free. I see you surrounded by the finest men of your kingdom, whose thoughts echo my greeting. Let me hear their voices joined with mine: Hail, King of Scotland!
ALL. Hail, King of Scotland!
[Flourish.]

MALCOLM. We shall not waste much time before we repay each of you for your love and loyalty. My thanes and kinsmen, from this day forward, be earls, the first that Scotland has ever honored with that title. What else remains to be done, what should be newly established in this new era, such as calling home our exiled friends who fled the traps of watchful tyranny, bringing to justice the cruel agents of this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen, who, it is believed, took her own life by her own violent hand, all this, and whatever else is called for, we will carry out in proper measure, time, and place. So, thanks to all at once and to each one of you, whom we invite to come and see us crowned at Scone.
[Flourish. Exeunt.]
